claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios and selected platinum-group-metal substitutes.
Post-synthesis annealing at approximately 300–350 °C in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere containing low-ppm H2O and NO is the proposed intervention.
Conditions of 300–350 °C with low-ppm H2O and NO are representative of transient, low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation.
The controlled oxidation treatment will form an ultrathin, self-assembled high-entropy oxide skin on the alloy catalyst.
The proposed oxide skin will be enriched in oxidation-prone elements such as Cr and Mn.
The treatment will not significantly alter the underlying bulk catalyst composition.
The oxide skin will passivate the alloy surface against further dealloying.
The oxide skin will inhibit catalyst sintering during thermal aging.
The ultrathin oxide layer will retain accessible active sites for reactant adsorption.
The treated catalyst will have greater durability than the untreated catalyst under prolonged transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The treated catalyst will sustain higher catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst under prolonged transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The treatment will enable lower overall platinum-group-metal consumption than the untreated starting catalyst.
The untreated starting catalyst loses activity and durability during exposure to H2O, NO, and thermal cycling.
Dealloying contributes to the untreated catalyst's degradation.
Sintering contributes to the untreated catalyst's activity loss.
Over-oxidation can produce an excessively passivating oxide layer that blocks active sites and negates the treatment benefit.
The optimal temperature, time, and gas-composition window for forming a protective but nonblocking oxide layer is uncertain.
